AITA for refusing to attend my friend's second wedding and being unsupportive overall? | Excuse me if I make any mistakes. I was the bridesmaid for the wedding between Dia and Jake. I have known both of them since I was little, in fact, I was the one who introduced them to each other. Dia was my neighbor and Jake was the son of my mother's colleague, they were like brother and sister to me and we have been close. After dating for 6 years and married for 2 years, Jake passed away suddenly from a fever last March. This year January, Dia announced that she was to be married again, and she wanted me to attend her wedding, date is not set but very likely in a couple of months. I had no idea that Dia even had another boyfriend till she announced it despite being close to her. It was barely a year after Jake's death I could not believe nor accept that she was already having her second marriage. When I tried to ask, Dia only said that she was going to move forward and leave the painful memories behind. I turned down the invitation. Dia was upset that I couldn't be supportive for her new found happiness, she said that I am important to her and she wanted me to be there for her, to show her the love and support like when she and Jake got together. I couldn't. I love Dia, and I love Jake too. It just didn't sit well with me that Dia moved on so quickly and I was angry at her and felt sorry for Jake. Jake and Dia are the only true couple in my eyes. Her friends are saying that I am being selfish making it all about myself and not for the bride, that I should be a true friend and be happy and supportive for her. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: <0> **Why:** - **Your feelings are valid.** Grief is deeply personal, and 10 months after a spouse’s death is not an arbitrary "deadline" for moving on. What feels "too quick" to you is entirely subjective and rooted in your emotional attachment to both Jake and Dia. You’re not obligated to celebrate a new marriage that conflicts with your unresolved grief for Jake—especially since you were so close to him. - **Refusing attendance ≠ being unsupportive.** You can love Dia and still not attend her wedding. Support isn’t limited to physical presence at an event; it could mean offering comfort in other ways (e.g., coffee, listening) or giving yourself space to process. Forcing yourself to attend out of guilt could harm *your* healing. - **The "selfish" accusation is misplaced.** True friendship respects boundaries, even when painful. Dia’s expectation that you "be happy for her" ignores that her happiness for this new relationship may clash with your grief for Jake. Her friends’ pressure ("make it about yourself") is invalidating—your pain isn’t selfish; it’s human. - **Context matters.** You introduced them, were like family, and Jake’s death is fresh in your memory. It’s reasonable to feel conflicted about Dia remarrying so soon. No one has a right to demand you suppress your emotions for their comfort. **Important nuance:** If you’ve *actively shamed* Dia, spread negativity about her new relationship, or refused to engage with her at all, that could cross into unkindness. But based on your description, you simply declined the invitation—no aggression, no hostility. That’s not AITA; it’s self-preservation. **What to do next:** - Communicate gently to Dia: *"I love you and Jake so much. This is hard for me, and I need time to process. I’m not here to hurt you—I just can’t be at the wedding right now, but I care about you deeply."* - Seek support for *yourself* (therapy, grief groups). Grief for a loss like Jake’s can be complex, especially when the person you loved is moving on. - Remember: Your worth isn’t tied to her wedding. You’re allowed to honor your feelings without being "wrong." *(Note: This isn’t about "right/wrong" in a moral sense—it’s about whether your reaction is unreasonable. In this case, it’s not.)*
